```{r, include = FALSE}
have_pkgs <- all(vapply(
  c("AER", "fixest", "quantreg", "estimatr", "sandwich", "clubSandwich"),
  requireNamespace,
  logical(1),
  quietly = TRUE
))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = have_pkgs
)
options(width = 110)

build_rich_tables <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
have_gt <- have_pkgs && requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
source("_pkgdown-helpers.R")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(spicy)
library(AER) # ivreg(), tobit(), bptest() and the three data sets
library(fixest) # feols(), fepois(), fenegbin()
library(quantreg) # rq()
library(estimatr) # lm_robust(), iv_robust()
```

This article covers robust and clustered standard errors on an `lm()`,
their counterparts in `estimatr::lm_robust()`, fixed-effects models
with fixest, instrumental variables, the tobit model and quantile
regression. The companion article [*Publication-ready
regression tables*](table-regression.html) covers the shared mechanics
(output engines, labels, `tidy()`), and the class-by-class map is
[*Supported models*](table-regression-supported-models.html).

## Two kinds of trouble

The estimators of this article answer two different problems.

In the first, the coefficients of least squares are fine and their
standard errors are not. The errors have unequal variances, or the
observations come in groups whose members resemble each other. A
robust variance repairs the standard errors, the intervals and the
tests, and leaves the coefficients as they are.

In the second, the coefficient itself is in question. A predictor is
correlated with what the model leaves out, the outcome is censored, or
the effect differs between the bottom and the top of the distribution.
The answer is another estimator: fixed effects, instrumental
variables, tobit, quantile regression.

A table has to say which estimator and which variance it reports.
`table_regression()` writes both under the table, in every case below.

## The data

Three data sets of the AER package carry the examples. `CPS1988` is a
cross-section of 28,155 employed American men, with wage, education,
experience and ethnicity. `Fatalities` is a panel of the 48 contiguous
states from 1982 to 1988, with traffic deaths and the tax on beer.
`PSID1976` holds 753 married women, their hours of paid work, and for
the 428 who work, their wage.

```{r data}
data("CPS1988", package = "AER")
data("Fatalities", package = "AER")
data("PSID1976", package = "AER")

Fatalities$frate <- with(Fatalities, fatal / pop * 10000) # deaths per 10,000
PSID1976$nwincome <- with(PSID1976, (fincome - hours * wage) / 1000)
working <- subset(PSID1976, participation == "yes")
```

## Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors

A wage equation on the CPS: the log wage on experience, its square,
education and ethnicity.

```{r hc-classical}
fit_wage <- lm(
  log(wage) ~ experience + I(experience^2) + education + ethnicity,
  data = CPS1988
)
bptest(fit_wage)
```

The Breusch-Pagan test leaves no doubt about the unequal variances.
`vcov =` asks for a robust estimator, and a list of fits with a list
of estimators puts the two sets of standard errors side by side.

```{r hc-side-by-side}
table_regression(
  list(Classical = fit_wage, HC3 = fit_wage),
  vcov = list("classical", "HC3"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci"),
  digits = 3
)
```

The coefficients are the same in both columns. The robust standard
errors are larger, by 24% for the square of experience and by 8% for
education.

`"HC0"` to `"HC3"` differ by how they weight the squared residuals
when the sample is small. Zeileis (2004, p. 4) reports the conclusion
of the simulations of Long and Ervin: HC3 "provides the best
performance in small samples as it gives less weight to influential
observations". With 28,155 rows the four estimators agree to three
digits, and the choice no longer matters. `table_regression()` keeps
the classical variance as its default and computes a robust one only
on request.

## `vcov =` or `lm_robust()`

`estimatr::lm_robust()` chooses the variance at fit time. The table
reports the standard errors of the fit, and they are those that
`vcov =` gives on an `lm()`.

```{r hc-lm-robust}
fit_wage_rob <- lm_robust(
  log(wage) ~ experience + I(experience^2) + education + ethnicity,
  data = CPS1988, se_type = "HC3"
)

table_regression(
  list("lm(), HC3" = fit_wage, "lm_robust(), HC3" = fit_wage_rob),
  vcov = list("HC3", "classical"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"),
  digits = 4
)
```

For a fit that carries its own variance, `"classical"` means the
variance of the fit. One difference deserves attention: without
`se_type`, estimatr computes HC2, where an `lm()` table is classical.
The note says which one is in the table.

```{r hc-lm-robust-default}
table_regression(lm_robust(frate ~ beertax, data = Fatalities))
```

## Clustered standard errors

The 336 rows of `Fatalities` are 48 states observed seven times. Two
years of the same state resemble each other more than two states do,
and a variance that treats the rows as independent is too small. A
cluster-robust variance takes the state as the unit.

```{r cluster-pooled}
pooled <- lm(frate ~ beertax, data = Fatalities)

table_regression(
  list(Classical = pooled, HC3 = pooled, CR1 = pooled, CR2 = pooled),
  vcov = list("classical", "HC3", "CR1", "CR2"),
  cluster = list(NULL, NULL, ~state, ~state),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci", "p")
)
```

The coefficient of the beer tax keeps its value, and its p-value moves
from below .001 to .019 under CR1 and .036 under CR2. Correcting for
heteroskedasticity alone (HC3) changes little: the trouble here is the
dependence within states.

`"CR1"` is the sandwich with the correction G / (G − 1) for G
clusters, `"CR1S"` the variant of Stata, and `"CR2"` the adjustment of
Bell and McCaffrey (2002). Under `"CR1"` and `"CR2"` the tests are t
tests with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, computed for each
coefficient. `lm_robust()` with `clusters =` gives the same numbers:

```{r cluster-estimatr-same}
table_regression(
  list(
    "lm(), CR2" = pooled,
    "lm_robust(), CR2" = lm_robust(
      frate ~ beertax,
      data = Fatalities, clusters = state, se_type = "CR2"
    )
  ),
  vcov = list("CR2", "classical"),
  cluster = list(~state, NULL),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "df", "p"),
  digits = 3
)
```

The `df` column prints the degrees of freedom of each test.

## Few clusters

A cluster-robust variance is justified when the clusters are many.
Cameron, Gelbach and Miller (2008) show that the usual tests reject
too often with few clusters, five to thirty in their study. The
number of clusters is not the whole story either. Bell and McCaffrey
(2002, p. 169) note that the bias is large "when the number of PSUs
is small or a coefficient depends primarily on data from a small
number of PSUs". In the previous table, the beer tax has 5.2 degrees
of freedom under CR2, with 48 states. Imbens and Kolesár (2016) trace
such losses to a regressor whose distribution is skewed across
clusters.

The CPS has four regions. Clustering a wage equation on them shows
what four clusters can and cannot support. The example draws 2,000
men, since CR2 forms one matrix per cluster and four clusters of
7,000 rows take minutes.

```{r few-clusters}
set.seed(1988)
cps <- CPS1988[sample(nrow(CPS1988), 2000), ]
fit_cps <- lm(
  log(wage) ~ experience + I(experience^2) + education + ethnicity,
  data = cps
)

table_regression(
  list(Classical = fit_cps, CR1 = fit_cps, CR1S = fit_cps, CR2 = fit_cps),
  vcov = list("classical", "CR1", "CR1S", "CR2"),
  cluster = list(NULL, ~region, ~region, ~region),
  keep = c("education", "ethnicity"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci", "p"),
  digits = 3
)
```

For the wage gap of African-American men, the three clustered
columns give p = .044, .029 and .099. They differ by their standard
error and by their reference distribution: 2.4 Satterthwaite degrees
of freedom under CR1, G − 1 = 3 under CR1S, 1.9 under CR2. Imbens and
Kolesár (2016) and Pustejovsky and Tipton (2018) recommend CR2 with
its degrees of freedom as the routine choice. With four clusters,
that choice rests on fewer than two degrees of freedom: these data
cannot settle the question at the level of the region.

## Panel data: the within estimator

In the pooled regression above, states with a higher beer tax have
more traffic deaths. States differ in many ways that the model
ignores, and a panel allows a comparison of each state with itself.
Fixed effects for state and year do that, either as dummy variables
in an `lm()` or absorbed by `fixest::feols()`.

```{r panel-pooled-lsdv-within}
lsdv <- lm(frate ~ beertax + state + year, data = Fatalities)
within <- feols(frate ~ beertax | state + year, data = Fatalities)

table_regression(
  list(Pooled = pooled, "Dummies (LSDV)" = lsdv, "Within (feols)" = within),
  keep = "beertax",
  show_intercept = FALSE
)
```

The sign reverses: 0.36 in the pooled model, −0.64 within states. The
dummy-variable model and `feols()` are one estimator computed two
ways, and they agree on the coefficient and on its classical standard
error. The fixest column carries a block that says which effects were
absorbed. `keep` selects the rows of the predictors, and
`show_intercept` governs the intercept apart.

The price of the within estimator is known. Because the state effects
"account for all the higher-level variance, no other variables
measured at the higher level can be identified" (Bell, Fairbrother &
Jones, 2019, p. 1060): a characteristic of a state that does not
change over the seven years has no coefficient.

`show_fit_stats` adds the statistics specific to these models, the
number of groups and the within R².

```{r panel-fe-stats}
table_regression(
  within,
  show_fit_stats = c("fixed_effects", "nobs", "n_groups", "r2", "within_r2")
)
```

The model explains 91% of the variance of the death rate, almost all
of it through the fixed effects: the beer tax accounts for 4% of the
variation left within states and years.

## The variance of a fixest fit

Like estimatr, fixest sets the variance in the fit, with `vcov =` or
`cluster =` in `feols()`. The table reports it and names it.

```{r panel-vcov-at-fit}
within_cl <- feols(
  frate ~ beertax | state + year,
  data = Fatalities, cluster = ~state
)
within_tw <- feols(
  frate ~ beertax | state + year,
  data = Fatalities, vcov = "twoway"
)
within_dk <- feols(
  frate ~ beertax | state + year,
  data = Fatalities, panel.id = ~ state + year, vcov = "DK"
)

table_regression(
  list(
    IID = within, "Cluster state" = within_cl,
    "Two-way" = within_tw, "Driscoll-Kraay" = within_dk
  ),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
```

The coefficient is the same in the four columns, and its p-value is
.001, .080, .092 and .012. The estimators of `table_regression()` are
refused for a fixest fit, with the way to obtain them in fixest:

```{r panel-refusal, error = TRUE}
table_regression(within, vcov = "HC3")
```

Clustered standard errors of the same model do not agree to the last
digit across software, because the small-sample corrections differ.
The dummy-variable `lm()` under three estimators, next to fixest:

```{r panel-cluster}
table_regression(
  list(
    "LSDV, CR1" = lsdv, "LSDV, CR1S" = lsdv, "LSDV, CR2" = lsdv,
    "feols, cluster" = within_cl
  ),
  vcov = list("CR1", "CR1S", "CR2", "classical"),
  cluster = list(~state, ~state, ~state, NULL),
  keep = "beertax",
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci", "p"),
  digits = 3
)
```

fixest counts fewer parameters than Stata's formula applied to the
dummy-variable model, since it leaves out the fixed effects nested in
the clusters (`?fixest::ssc`). With `ssc(K.fixef = "full")` it
returns the CR1S column. The four p-values lie between .08 and .13.
The classical one was .001.

## Fixed-effects count models

Deaths are counts, and the population at risk differs widely between
states. A Poisson model with the population as exposure
and the same two fixed effects is `fepois()`, and `fenegbin()` relaxes
the equality of mean and variance.

```{r fepois}
fp <- fepois(
  fatal ~ beertax | state + year,
  offset = ~ log(pop), data = Fatalities, cluster = ~state
)
fnb <- fenegbin(
  fatal ~ beertax | state + year,
  offset = ~ log(pop), data = Fatalities, cluster = ~state
)

table_regression(
  list(Poisson = fp, "Negative binomial" = fnb),
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_fit_stats = c("fixed_effects", "nobs", "theta", "pseudo_r2_mcfadden", "aic")
)
```

`exponentiate = TRUE` gives incidence rate ratios: one more unit of the
tax on a case of beer goes with a death rate multiplied by 0.71 in the
Poisson model, 95% CI [0.52, 0.96].

Average marginal effects are available for `feols()` and for a GLM
without fixed effects. For a GLM with fixed effects they are refused,
and the message gives the reason.

```{r fepois-ame-refused, error = TRUE}
table_regression(fp, show_columns = c("b", "ame"))
```

## Instrumental variables

The return to a year of education is the textbook case of a
coefficient in doubt: ability raises both schooling and wages, and
least squares credits schooling with both. An instrument is a
variable that moves education and has no other path to the wage. The
example takes the education of the father and of the mother, for the
428 working women of the PSID.

Of the assumptions behind an instrument, one can be checked. For
Gelman, Hill and Vehtari (2020, p. 431), the correlation of the
instrument with the treatment "is the only assumption that can be
directly tested", and the first-stage model "should be examined
closely to assess the strength of the instrument". The first stage is
an ordinary `lm()`, and its table comes first.

```{r iv-first-stage}
first <- lm(
  education ~ feducation + meducation + experience + I(experience^2),
  data = working
)
table_regression(
  first,
  vcov = "HC1",
  keep = c("feducation", "meducation"),
  digits = 3
)
```

Both parents' education predict the daughter's. The tests of weak
instruments, of endogeneity and of overidentification have no place
in the table. They come from `summary()` of the fit, and `note_add`
can carry them.

```{r iv-diagnostics}
iv <- ivreg(
  log(wage) ~ education + experience + I(experience^2) |
    feducation + meducation + experience + I(experience^2),
  data = working
)
summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)$diagnostics
```

The second stage is not an `lm()` on the fitted values of the first:
"the standard-error calculation is complicated because we cannot
simply look at the second regression in isolation" (Gelman et al.,
2020, p. 429). `AER::ivreg()`, `estimatr::iv_robust()` and
`fixest::feols()` do the calculation, and their fits go in one table
with the least-squares model.

```{r iv-table}
ols_w <- lm(
  log(wage) ~ education + experience + I(experience^2),
  data = working
)
iv_rob <- iv_robust(
  log(wage) ~ education + experience + I(experience^2) |
    feducation + meducation + experience + I(experience^2),
  data = working, se_type = "HC1"
)
iv_fe <- feols(
  log(wage) ~ experience + I(experience^2) |
    education ~ feducation + meducation,
  data = working, vcov = "hetero"
)

table_regression(
  list(OLS = ols_w, "ivreg()" = iv, "iv_robust()" = iv_rob, "feols()" = iv_fe),
  vcov = list("HC1", "classical", "classical", "classical"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = "nobs",
  digits = 3
)
```

The return to a year of education falls from 0.107 to 0.061, and its
standard error more than doubles: an instrument uses only a part of
the variation of education. The three implementations give the same
coefficient.

An `ivreg()` fit takes `vcov = "HC0"` and `"HC1"`, and the
cluster-robust estimators `"CR0"` to `"CR3"` and `"CR1S"` with a
`cluster`. The values are those of `iv_robust()`.

```{r iv-robust}
table_regression(
  list("ivreg(), HC1" = iv, "iv_robust(), HC1" = iv_rob),
  vcov = list("HC1", "classical"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = "nobs",
  digits = 3
)
```

`"HC2"` to `"HC5"` are refused. They weight each residual by its
leverage, which AER and estimatr do not define the same way for
two-stage least squares, and the error says so.

```{r iv-refusal, error = TRUE}
table_regression(iv, vcov = "HC3")
```

## Censored outcomes: tobit

Of the 753 women, 325 did not work for pay in 1975: their hours are
zero. Least squares on all the rows treats these zeros as ordinary
values. The tobit model posits a latent variable, here the desired
hours, that is observed only when it is positive (Gelman et al.,
2020, p. 284).

```{r tobit}
tob <- tobit(
  hours ~ nwincome + education + experience + I(experience^2) + age +
    youngkids + oldkids,
  data = PSID1976
)
ols_h <- lm(
  hours ~ nwincome + education + experience + I(experience^2) + age +
    youngkids + oldkids,
  data = PSID1976
)

table_regression(
  list("OLS (zeros included)" = ols_h, Tobit = tob),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "sigma", "aic")
)
```

The tobit coefficient of education is 80.65 hours per year of
schooling, against 28.76 by least squares. The two do not measure the
same thing. A tobit coefficient is a slope of the latent variable. The
slope of the observed hours is smaller, since part of the women stay
at zero whatever the change.

The same holds for the average marginal effects of a tobit fit: they
are average slopes of the latent variable, and the note under the
table says so.

```{r tobit-ame}
table_regression(
  tob,
  show_columns = c("b", "ame", "ame_ci"),
  keep = c("education", "experience", "youngkids")
)
```

For education the AME repeats the coefficient, and for experience it
takes the squared term into account. `vcov = "CR1"` with a `cluster`
is the one robust estimator of a tobit fit.

## Quantile regression

Least squares models the mean of the outcome. Quantile regression
models a quantile, and several quantiles show whether a predictor
acts in the same way at the bottom and at the top of the
distribution. `quantreg::rq()` fits one quantile at a time. A table
of several quantiles takes a list of fits, one per `tau`.

```{r rq-mean-quantiles}
q10 <- rq(
  log(wage) ~ experience + I(experience^2) + education + ethnicity,
  tau = 0.10, data = CPS1988
)
q50 <- update(q10, tau = 0.50)
q90 <- update(q10, tau = 0.90)

table_regression(
  list(Mean = fit_wage, Q10 = q10, Median = q50, Q90 = q90),
  vcov = list("HC3", "classical", "classical", "classical"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se"),
  digits = 3
)
```

The wage gap of African-American men is −0.283 at the first
decile and −0.207 at the ninth: it narrows toward the top. The return
to experience falls from 0.102 to 0.056. The return to education
changes little, from 0.082 to 0.093. The standard error of the gap is
nearly twice as large at the first decile as at the median: outer
quantiles are harder to estimate (Harrell, 2015, p. 360).

The variance of a quantile regression has its own estimators, since
it depends on the density of the outcome around the quantile. The
tokens are those of quantreg. For an `rq` fit, `"classical"` is
`"nid"`, the sandwich that allows unequal densities.

```{r rq-vcov, warning = FALSE}
q50_cps <- rq(
  log(wage) ~ experience + I(experience^2) + education + ethnicity,
  tau = 0.5, data = cps
)

set.seed(2)
table_regression(
  list(nid = q50_cps, iid = q50_cps, ker = q50_cps, bootstrap = q50_cps),
  vcov = list("nid", "iid", "ker", "bootstrap"),
  boot_n = 500,
  keep = c("education", "ethnicity"),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci"),
  digits = 3
)
```

`summary()` of quantreg does not default to `"nid"` on a small sample:
below 1,001 rows it inverts a rank test (`?summary.rq`). That method
gives confidence intervals without standard errors, and
`vcov = "rank"` reproduces it: the standard errors and the p-values of
the table stay empty.

For clustered data, `vcov = "bootstrap"` with a `cluster` runs the
wild gradient bootstrap of Hagemann (2017). The median death rate of
the panel, clustered by state:

```{r rq-cluster-bootstrap, warning = FALSE}
q_frate <- rq(frate ~ beertax + year, tau = 0.5, data = Fatalities)

set.seed(3)
table_regression(
  list(nid = q_frate, "Cluster bootstrap" = q_frate),
  vcov = list("nid", "bootstrap"),
  cluster = list(NULL, ~state),
  boot_n = 500,
  keep = "beertax",
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci", "p"),
  digits = 3
)
```

The standard error of the beer tax is more than three times larger
once the states are taken as clusters. The method assumes many clusters.
Hagemann (2017) reports that with very few of them, inference from
bootstrap standard errors rejects too often.

One argument can mislead a user of quantreg. In `table_regression()`,
`tau` is the time horizon of the survival columns. The quantile of a
fit is set in `rq(tau = )`.

## Presentation-ready output

Everything above renders through the rich output engines. The three
models of the beer tax, with standard errors clustered by state, as a
`gt` table:

```{r rich, eval = build_rich_tables && have_gt}
pkgdown_dark_gt(
  table_regression(
    list(Pooled = pooled, "Dummies (LSDV)" = lsdv, "Within" = within_cl),
    vcov = list("CR2", "CR2", "classical"),
    cluster = list(~state, ~state, NULL),
    keep = "beertax",
    output = "gt"
  )
)
```

  effects models: Making an informed choice. *Quality & Quantity*,
  53(2), 1051--1074.

  errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. *Survey
  Methodology*, 28(2), 169--181.
* Cameron, A. C., Gelbach, J. B., & Miller, D. L. (2008).
  Bootstrap-based improvements for inference with clustered errors.
  *Review of Economics and Statistics*, 90(3), 414--427.
* Gelman, A., Hill, J., & Vehtari, A. (2020). *Regression and other
  stories*. Cambridge University Press.
* Hagemann, A. (2017). Cluster-robust bootstrap inference in quantile
  regression models. *Journal of the American Statistical
  Association*, 112(517), 446--456.
* Harrell, F. E. (2015). *Regression modeling strategies: With
  applications to linear models, logistic and ordinal regression, and
  survival analysis* (2nd ed.). Springer.
* Imbens, G. W., & Kolesár, M. (2016). Robust standard errors in small
  samples: Some practical advice. *Review of Economics and
  Statistics*, 98(4), 701--712.
* Pustejovsky, J. E., & Tipton, E. (2018). Small-sample methods for
  cluster-robust variance estimation and hypothesis testing in fixed
  effects models. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 36(4),
  672--683.
